subject: Physics
title: Moving Charges and Magnetism
summary: A moving charge or a current produces a magnetic field, and a magnetic field pushes on moving charges and currents. This chapter builds both halves: the Lorentz force and the motion of a charge in a field, then the Biot–Savart law and Ampere's circuital law for the fields of a straight wire, a circular loop and a solenoid, and finally the force between parallel currents, the torque on a current loop and the moving coil galvanometer. It is the first half of Unit III (Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism) and one of the most derivation-heavy chapters of the paper.

exam_profile.weightage: Unit III (Chapters 4 and 5) together with Unit IV (Chapters 6 and 7) carries 17 marks in the CBSE Class 12 Physics paper. This chapter typically contributes about 7 to 9 marks: usually one 5-mark or 3-mark derivation (circular loop, solenoid, parallel wires, torque or galvanometer), one numerical on a moving charge or a wire in a field, and one or two 1-mark questions.

question_types.note: Radius, time period or ratio of radii of charges in a magnetic field; the quantity that stays constant (kinetic energy); field at the centre of a loop, arc or solenoid; whether parallel wires attract or repel; unit of B; shunt or series resistance for converting a galvanometer.
Magnetic force does no work; a charge moving parallel to B feels no force; the field inside a long solenoid is uniform; why a galvanometer has a linear scale; why parallel currents attract.

Define the ampere or tesla; compare radii of an electron and a proton with the same energy or momentum; why the galvanometer field is radial; direction of force on a beam of electrons; a two-line numerical with F = BIl sinθ or r = mv/qB.

Ampere's law for a straight wire or inside a thick wire with the B–r graph; the solenoid derivation; force on one side of a rectangular loop near a straight wire; converting a galvanometer into an ammeter or voltmeter; field at the centre of two concentric or coaxial coils.

Derive the field on the axis of a circular loop using the Biot–Savart law; derive the force between parallel currents and define the ampere; derive the torque on a rectangular loop and the magnetic moment; principle, construction, working and sensitivity of a moving coil galvanometer, usually with a small numerical attached.
A passage on the moving coil galvanometer or on the circular motion of a charge in a magnetic field, followed by four short parts including one two-step numerical.

sections.heading: 4.2 Magnetic Force: Sources and Fields, Lorentz Force
sections.body:
Oersted's compass experiment (1820) showed that a current deflects a magnetic needle, and Ampere's later work established that all magnetism has moving charges behind it. So the chapter is built on one pair of statements: moving charges produce a magnetic field B, and a magnetic field exerts a force on moving charges. Like the electric field, B is a vector field defined at every point, it obeys superposition, and it is produced by currents. Unlike E, it acts only on charges that move.

A charge q moving with velocity v in a region where both an electric field E and a magnetic field B exist experiences the Lorentz force F = q(E + v × B). The magnetic part Fm = q(v × B) has three properties the examiner expects you to state. It depends on q, v and B and is proportional to each; it vanishes when the charge is at rest or moves parallel or antiparallel to B (sin θ = 0); and it is always perpendicular to both v and B, so it can bend the path but never change the speed. Because the force is perpendicular to the displacement at every instant, the work done by a magnetic force on a charge is always zero and its kinetic energy stays constant.

The direction comes from the right-hand rule for the cross product: point the fingers along v, curl them towards B, and the thumb gives v × B. For a positive charge the force is along the thumb; for an electron it is opposite. The SI unit of B is the tesla (T): a field of 1 T exerts a force of 1 N on a charge of 1 C moving at 1 m s−1 perpendicular to the field, so 1 T = 1 N A−1 m−1. A smaller unit is the gauss, 1 G = 10−4 T; the earth's field is about 3.6 × 10−5 T.

formulas.expr: F = q(E + v × B); magnitude of magnetic part F = qvB sin θ
where: magnetic field (T); 1 T = 1 N A<sup>−1</sup> m<sup>−1</sup> = 10<sup>4</sup> G

sections.tip: Whenever a question asks for the direction of the force on an electron, first find v × B for a positive charge and then reverse it. Half the wrong answers in this chapter come from forgetting the negative sign of the electron.

sections.heading: 4.2.3 Magnetic Force on a Current-Carrying Conductor
sections.body:
A current is a stream of moving charges, so a wire carrying a current in a magnetic field feels a force. Take a straight conductor of length l and cross-section A with n free electrons per unit volume, each drifting with velocity vd. The total mobile charge is q = (nAl)e, and the force on all of it is F = (nAle)(vd × B). Since the current is I = neAvd, this becomes F = I (l × B), where l is a vector of magnitude l along the direction of the current. The magnitude is F = BIl sin θ, θ being the angle between the wire and the field. The force is maximum (BIl) when the wire is perpendicular to the field and zero when it lies along the field.

For a wire of arbitrary shape, add the forces on its elements: F = ∑ I dl × B. In a uniform field this sum depends only on the vector joining the two ends, which gives two useful results: a closed loop in a uniform field experiences no net force (though it may experience a torque), and a curved wire between two points feels the same force as a straight wire joining them.

The direction can be found with Fleming's left-hand rule: hold the forefinger, middle finger and thumb of the left hand mutually perpendicular; forefinger along B, middle finger along the current, and the thumb gives the force. NCERT Example 4.1 is the standard application: a wire of mass 200 g and length 1.5 m carrying 2 A floats in a horizontal field when BIl = mg, giving B = 0.2 × 9.8/(2 × 1.5) = 0.65 T, with the field horizontal and perpendicular to the wire.

where: length of the conductor inside the field (m)
angle between the current direction and B

sections.tip: In F = BIl sin θ the angle is between the wire and the field. If the question says the wire makes 30° with the field, use sin 30°; do not swap to cos.

sections.heading: 4.3 Motion in a Magnetic Field
sections.body:
Because the magnetic force is always perpendicular to the velocity, it acts as a pure deflecting force: it changes the direction of v but not its magnitude. Consider a charge q moving with speed v perpendicular to a uniform field B. The force qvB is perpendicular to v and constant in magnitude, which is exactly the condition for uniform circular motion. Equating it to the centripetal force, qvB = mv2/r, so the radius is r = mv/(qB). The larger the momentum, the larger the circle; the stronger the field, the tighter the circle.

The angular frequency is ω = v/r = qB/m and the time period is T = 2πr/v = 2πm/(qB). Both are independent of the speed and of the radius: a fast particle moves on a bigger circle but completes it in the same time as a slow one. The frequency ν = qB/(2πm) is called the cyclotron frequency. This independence is what allowed the cyclotron to accelerate particles with an alternating voltage of fixed frequency.

If the velocity makes an angle θ with B, resolve it. The component v sin θ perpendicular to the field produces circular motion of radius r = mv sin θ/(qB); the component v cos θ along the field is unaffected, so the particle drifts along the field while it circles. The path is a helix with its axis along B. The distance moved along the field in one revolution is the pitch, p = (v cos θ) T = 2πmv cos θ/(qB). A charge moving parallel to B feels no force and continues in a straight line.

Two comparisons recur in the paper. For the same speed, r ∝ m/q, so an alpha particle (m = 4mp, q = 2e) has twice the radius of a proton. For the same kinetic energy K, r = √(2mK)/(qB), so a proton and an alpha particle of equal energy have equal radii, while a deuteron has √2 times the proton's radius.

formulas.expr: r = mv/(qB), ω = qB/m, T = 2πm/(qB), ν = qB/(2πm)
where: time period, independent of v and r

formulas.expr: Pitch of helix p = v cos θ · T = 2πmv cos θ/(qB)
where: velocity component along the field, unchanged by the force

sections.tip: For same-energy questions write r = √(2mK)/(qB) before comparing; for same-momentum questions r = p/(qB), so the radius depends only on charge. State which case applies in the first line of your answer.

sections.heading: 4.4 Magnetic Field due to a Current Element, Biot–Savart Law
sections.body:
The Biot–Savart law is the magnetic counterpart of Coulomb's law: it gives the field produced by a small element of current. Consider a conductor carrying a steady current I and a small element dl of it, pointing along the current. At a point P whose position vector from the element is r, the field is dB = (μ0/4π) · I (dl × r)/r3. In magnitude, dB = (μ0/4π) · I dl sin θ/r2, where θ is the angle between dl and r. The direction of dB is perpendicular to the plane containing dl and r, given by the right-hand rule for the cross product; for a straight wire this means the field circles the wire.

Points to state, because they carry marks: the field is directly proportional to the current, to the length of the element and to sin θ, and inversely proportional to the square of the distance. It is zero at points along the line of the element (θ = 0 or 180°) and maximum in the plane perpendicular to it (θ = 90°). The constant μ0/4π = 10−7 T m A−1, so μ0 = 4π × 10−7 T m A−1, the permeability of free space. The total field of a conductor is the vector sum (integral) of the contributions of all its elements; that is the principle of superposition applied to B.

Comparison with Coulomb's law is a standard 2-mark question. Both are long range and fall as 1/r2; both obey superposition. The differences: the electrostatic field is produced by a scalar source (charge) while the magnetic field is produced by a vector source (I dl); the electric field is along the line joining source and point, while the magnetic field is perpendicular to the plane containing the element and that line; and the magnetic field has the angle dependence sin θ, being zero along the element.

formulas.expr: dB = (μ0/4π) · I (dl × r)/r3; dB = (μ0/4π) · I dl sin θ/r2
where: permeability of free space, 4π × 10<sup>−7</sup> T m A<sup>−1</sup>
vector from the element to the point

sections.tip: Always draw the element, the position vector and the angle θ before writing the law; the vector form with dl × r earns the full mark, the scalar form alone may not.

sections.heading: 4.5 Magnetic Field on the Axis of a Circular Current Loop
sections.body:
This is the chapter's first flagship derivation. Take a circular loop of radius R carrying current I, centred at the origin with its plane in the y–z plane, and a point P on the axis at distance x from the centre. Pick an element dl on the loop. The distance from it to P is r = √(x2 + R2), and dl is perpendicular to r, so sin θ = 1 and dB = (μ0/4π) · I dl/(x2 + R2).

The direction of dB is perpendicular to both dl and r. Resolve it into a component dB cos α along the axis and dB sin α perpendicular to it, where α is the angle between r and the axis. For the diametrically opposite element the perpendicular component is reversed, so all perpendicular components cancel in pairs and only the axial components add. With cos α = R/√(x2 + R2), the axial component is dBx = (μ0/4π) · I dl R/(x2 + R2)3/2. Summing dl over the whole loop gives 2πR, so B = μ0IR2/[2(x2 + R2)3/2], directed along the axis.

Two limits matter. At the centre, x = 0 and B = μ0I/(2R); for a coil of N turns, B = μ0NI/(2R). Far away, x ≫ R and B ≈ μ0IR2/(2x3) = (μ0/4π) · 2m/x3 with m = IπR2, which is the same form as the axial field of an electric dipole; that is why a current loop is called a magnetic dipole. The direction of the field on the axis follows the right-hand thumb rule: curl the fingers of the right hand along the current and the thumb points along B at the centre. A current circulating anticlockwise, seen by the observer, gives a field towards the observer (a north face).

Fields of arcs follow at once from the centre formula. A semicircle gives μ0I/(4R); an arc subtending angle φ (in radians) gives μ0Iφ/(4πR). A long straight wire touching the arc contributes nothing at the centre if the centre lies on its line.

where: distance of the point from the centre along the axis

formulas.expr: B<sub>centre</sub> = μ<sub>0</sub>NI/(2R); arc of angle φ: B = μ<sub>0</sub>Iφ/(4πR)
where: angle subtended by the arc at the centre, in radians

sections.tip: The step the marking scheme looks for is the cancellation of the perpendicular components between diametrically opposite elements. Say it in words and show it in the figure; without it the derivation loses a mark.

sections.heading: 4.6 Ampere's Circuital Law
sections.body:
Ampere's circuital law is to magnetism what Gauss's law is to electrostatics: a statement about the field summed round a closed path. It says that the line integral of B around any closed loop equals μ0 times the total current passing through the surface bounded by the loop: ∮ B·dl = μ0Ienc. The loop is called an Amperian loop; it is a mathematical curve, not a physical wire. Currents outside the loop contribute to B at points on the loop but not to the integral. The sign of each current is fixed by the right-hand rule: with the fingers curling along the direction of traversal, currents along the thumb count positive.

The law is most useful when symmetry makes B constant in magnitude and tangential all along the loop, so that ∮ B·dl = B × (length of loop). For a long straight wire carrying current I, choose a circle of radius r centred on the wire: B(2πr) = μ0I, so B = μ0I/(2πr). The field circles the wire, falls as 1/r, and its direction is given by the right-hand thumb rule (thumb along the current, fingers curl along B).

The same method handles a thick wire of radius a with current I spread uniformly over its cross-section. Outside (r ≥ a) the loop encloses all of I, so B = μ0I/(2πr) as before. Inside (r < a) the enclosed current is I(r2/a2), so B(2πr) = μ0Ir2/a2, giving B = μ0Ir/(2πa2). The field grows linearly from zero at the axis to a maximum μ0I/(2πa) at the surface and then falls as 1/r. The B–r graph, a straight line up to r = a followed by a hyperbola-like fall, is asked frequently and should be drawn with the surface value marked.

Ampere's law is exact for steady currents but, like Gauss's law, it is easy to use only in symmetric cases: a long straight wire, a solenoid, a toroid. For a finite wire or a single loop one must go back to the Biot–Savart law.

where: net current threading the surface bounded by the loop, with signs from the right-hand rule

formulas.expr: Long straight wire: B = μ<sub>0</sub>I/(2πr); inside a thick wire: B = μ<sub>0</sub>Ir/(2πa<sup>2</sup>)

sections.tip: When a question gives several currents through a loop, add them with signs: a loop threaded by 3 A one way and 1 A the other has ∮ B·dl = μ<sub>0</sub> × 2 A, whatever the shape of the loop.

sections.heading: 4.7 The Solenoid
sections.body:
A solenoid is a long insulated wire wound closely in the form of a helix, so that each turn behaves like a circular loop. Inside a long solenoid the fields of neighbouring turns add to give a strong, uniform field parallel to the axis; outside, the fields of the upper and lower parts of the turns oppose each other and the field is very weak, essentially zero for an ideal (infinitely long) solenoid. Near the ends the field lines spread out; the solenoid behaves like a bar magnet with a north pole at the end where the current appears anticlockwise to an observer facing it.

The derivation with Ampere's law is a standard 3-mark answer. Let the solenoid have n turns per unit length and carry current I. Choose a rectangular Amperian loop abcd with side ab of length h inside and parallel to the axis, side cd outside, and sides bc and da perpendicular to the axis. Evaluate ∮ B·dl along the four sides. Along ab, B is parallel to dl and uniform, contributing Bh. Along bc and da, B is perpendicular to dl inside and zero outside, so they contribute nothing. Along cd the field is zero. Hence ∮ B·dl = Bh. The loop encloses nh turns, each carrying I, so Ienc = nhI. Ampere's law gives Bh = μ0nhI, that is B = μ0nI.

The result is independent of the radius of the solenoid and of the distance of the point from the axis, which is the meaning of a uniform field. It is increased by winding more turns per metre, by raising the current, or by filling the core with a ferromagnetic material of relative permeability μr, in which case B = μ0μrnI. At either end of a long solenoid the field drops to half, μ0nI/2, because only half of the turns lie on one side. For a solenoid of length L with N turns in total, n = N/L, and in NCERT exercise 4.8 the five layers of 400 turns on an 80 cm former give n = 2000/0.8 = 2500 m−1.

formulas.expr: B = μ<sub>0</sub>nI inside a long solenoid; B = μ<sub>0</sub>nI/2 at an end
where: number of turns per unit length, N/L (m<sup>−1</sup>)

sections.tip: Draw the rectangular loop with two sides parallel to the axis and say explicitly why three of the four sides contribute zero. The marking scheme allots a mark to that reasoning.

sections.heading: 4.8 Force between Two Parallel Currents, the Ampere
sections.body:
Two long straight parallel wires a and b, separated by distance d, carry currents Ia and Ib in the same direction. Wire a produces at the position of wire b a field Ba = μ0Ia/(2πd), directed perpendicular to b and into the plane (for a to the left of b with both currents upward). A length L of wire b, carrying Ib in this field, experiences the force Fba = IbLBa = μ0IaIbL/(2πd). By the rule F = I (L × B) this force is directed towards a. Repeating the argument for the force of b on a gives an equal force towards b: the wires attract. If one current is reversed the force reverses and the wires repel. So parallel currents attract, antiparallel currents repel, which is the opposite of the rule for charges.

The force per unit length on either wire is f = μ0IaIb/(2πd) = 2 × 10−7 IaIb/d in SI units. Putting Ia = Ib = 1 A and d = 1 m gives f = 2 × 10−7 N m−1. This is the NCERT definition of the ampere: one ampere is that steady current which, when maintained in each of two very long straight parallel conductors of negligible cross-section placed 1 m apart in vacuum, produces on each a force of 2 × 10−7 newton per metre of length. The coulomb follows as the charge carried past a point in one second by a current of one ampere.

Two things to note in the answer. The force on b due to a and the force on a due to b are equal and opposite here, as Newton's third law requires; NCERT points out that this need not hold in general for magnetic forces between isolated current elements. And because the force depends on the product of the currents and on 1/d, doubling both currents quadruples the force, while doubling the separation halves it.

where: force per unit length; attractive for parallel currents, repulsive for antiparallel

sections.tip: The definition of the ampere is worth 1 to 2 marks in most years. Write it with all its qualifiers: very long, straight, parallel, negligible cross-section, 1 m apart, in vacuum, 2 × 10<sup>−7</sup> N per metre.

sections.heading: 4.9 Torque on a Current Loop, Magnetic Dipole
sections.body:
A rectangular loop of sides a and b carrying current I is placed in a uniform field B. First take the field in the plane of the loop, parallel to the sides of length a. Those two sides carry current along or against B, so they feel no force. The sides of length b are perpendicular to B and carry current in opposite directions, so they feel equal and opposite forces F1 = F2 = IbB, directed into and out of the plane. Their lines of action are separated by a, so they form a couple of torque τ = F1(a/2) + F2(a/2) = IabB = IAB, where A = ab is the area. The net force is zero; the loop tends to rotate.

Now let the normal to the plane of the loop make an angle θ with B. The forces on the sides of length b are still IbB each, but the perpendicular distance between their lines of action is now a sin θ, so τ = IAB sin θ. The forces on the other two sides are equal, opposite and collinear, contributing nothing. For a coil of N turns, τ = NIAB sin θ. Defining the magnetic moment of the loop as m = NIA, with A along the normal by the right-hand rule (fingers along the current, thumb along m), the torque is τ = m × B. The torque is zero when the normal is along B (stable equilibrium at θ = 0, unstable at θ = 180°) and maximum, NIAB, when the plane of the loop is parallel to the field.

The magnetic moment has unit A m2 and behaves exactly like the electric dipole moment: τ = p × E becomes τ = m × B. The result holds for a planar loop of any shape, which is why NCERT exercise 4.13(b) says the torque does not change when a circular coil is reshaped into an irregular loop of the same area. A circular loop is likewise a magnetic dipole: its axial field far away, B = (μ0/4π) · 2m/x3, has the same form as the axial field of an electric dipole with 1/4πε0 replaced by μ0/4π and p by m. Unlike an electric dipole, however, a magnetic dipole cannot be split into two isolated poles.

where: angle between the normal to the loop (direction of m) and B

sections.tip: The angle in τ = NIAB sin θ is between the normal and the field. If a question says the plane of the coil makes 30° with B, the normal makes 60°, and you must use sin 60°.

sections.heading: 4.10 The Moving Coil Galvanometer
sections.body:
The moving coil galvanometer (MCG) is the chapter's main application and its most reliable 5-mark question. Principle: a current-carrying coil placed in a magnetic field experiences a torque. Construction: a coil of many turns of fine insulated wire wound on a light rectangular frame is suspended by a phosphor-bronze strip (or pivoted between springs) between the cylindrical pole pieces of a permanent magnet. A soft-iron cylinder is fixed inside the coil without touching it. The pole pieces are concave and, together with the soft-iron core, make the field radial: at every position of the coil the plane of the coil is parallel to the field lines, so sin θ = 1 always. The core also concentrates the field, making it stronger.

Working: when a current I flows, the magnetic torque NIAB turns the coil, twisting the suspension. The suspension provides a restoring torque kφ proportional to the twist φ, k being the torsion constant. At equilibrium NIAB = kφ, so φ = (NAB/k) I. The deflection is directly proportional to the current, which is why the scale is linear; a radial field is essential for this, because otherwise the magnetic torque would carry the factor sin θ and the scale would not be uniform.

Current sensitivity is the deflection per unit current, Is = φ/I = NAB/k. Voltage sensitivity is the deflection per unit voltage, Vs = φ/V = NAB/(kR), where R is the resistance of the coil. Both are raised by a large N, a large area, a strong field and a small k, which is why phosphor bronze, with its small torsion constant, is used. Increasing N to raise the current sensitivity does not necessarily raise the voltage sensitivity, because a longer wire also raises R; doubling N with the same wire doubles R and leaves Vs unchanged.

A galvanometer as such cannot measure current in a circuit: it is very sensitive, giving full-scale deflection for microamperes, and its resistance is not small enough to leave the circuit current unchanged. To convert it into an ammeter of range I, connect a small shunt resistance S in parallel so that only Ig passes through the coil: S = IgG/(I − Ig). The ammeter then has a very small resistance GS/(G + S) and is connected in series. To convert it into a voltmeter of range V, connect a large resistance R in series: R = V/Ig − G. The voltmeter has a large resistance G + R and is connected in parallel across the element.

formulas.expr: NIAB = kφ; I<sub>s</sub> = φ/I = NAB/k; V<sub>s</sub> = φ/V = NAB/(kR)
where: torsion constant of the suspension (N m rad<sup>−1</sup>)

formulas.expr: Shunt S = I<sub>g</sub>G/(I − I<sub>g</sub>); series resistance R = V/I<sub>g</sub> − G
where: required range of the ammeter or voltmeter

sections.tip: A neat labelled diagram (coil, soft-iron core, concave pole pieces, phosphor-bronze strip, mirror or pointer, spring) is usually worth one full mark of the five. Draw it even if the question does not ask for it.

key_terms.definition: The total force on a charge q moving with velocity v in electric and magnetic fields, F = q(E + v × B). The magnetic part is perpendicular to both v and B and does no work.

SI unit of magnetic field. A field of 1 T exerts a force of 1 N on a charge of 1 C moving at 1 m s<sup>−1</sup> perpendicular to the field; 1 T = 1 N A<sup>−1</sup> m<sup>−1</sup> = 10<sup>4</sup> gauss.
The frequency of revolution of a charge in a uniform magnetic field, ν = qB/(2πm). It is independent of the speed and the radius of the orbit.
The distance a charged particle moves along the field in one revolution when its velocity makes an angle with B: p = v cos θ · T = 2πmv cos θ/(qB).
The field of a current element I dl at a point at position r from it is dB = (μ0/4π) I (dl × r)/r3, proportional to I, dl and sin θ and inversely proportional to r2.
The constant μ<sub>0</sub> = 4π × 10<sup>−7</sup> T m A<sup>−1</sup> that fixes the strength of the magnetic field produced by a current in vacuum.
The line integral of B around any closed loop equals μ0 times the net current threading the loop: ∮ B·dl = μ0Ienc.
An imaginary closed curve chosen to apply Ampere's law, usually one along which B is constant in magnitude and tangential so that the integral reduces to B times the length.
A long wire wound closely as a helix. Inside a long solenoid the field is uniform, B = μ<sub>0</sub>nI, along the axis; outside it is nearly zero.

The steady current which, maintained in each of two very long straight parallel conductors of negligible cross-section placed 1 m apart in vacuum, produces on each a force of 2 × 10<sup>−7</sup> N per metre of length.
For a current loop, m = NIA, directed along the normal given by the right-hand rule. Unit A m2. The torque on the loop in a field is τ = m × B.

The field between the concave pole pieces and soft-iron core of a galvanometer, whose lines are always parallel to the plane of the coil, so the torque is NIAB for every deflection and the scale is linear.
Deflection of a galvanometer per unit current, φ/I = NAB/k, in rad A<sup>−1</sup> or div A<sup>−1</sup>.
Deflection per unit potential difference across the galvanometer, φ/V = NAB/(kR); it equals the current sensitivity divided by the coil resistance.
A small resistance connected in parallel with a galvanometer so that most of the current bypasses the coil, converting it into an ammeter: S = I<sub>g</sub>G/(I − I<sub>g</sub>).
The restoring torque per unit twist of a galvanometer suspension, k; the restoring torque is kφ. Phosphor bronze is used because its k is small.

diagrams.title: Circular and helical paths of a charge in a uniform magnetic field

Draw a positive charge entering with v perpendicular to B and trace a circle, marking the force qvB at two points pointing to the centre and the radius r = mv/qB. In a second sketch draw B along a horizontal axis and a helix around it, labelling the components v cos θ (along B) and v sin θ (perpendicular) and the pitch between successive turns.

Mark an element dl at the top of the loop, the vector r from dl to P (length √(x² + R²)), and dB perpendicular to r. Resolve dB into dB cos α along the axis and dB sin α perpendicular to it, and show the diametrically opposite element whose perpendicular component cancels. Write the final B = μ<sub>0</sub>IR²/2(x² + R²)<sup>3/2</sup> along the axis.

Superimpose a rectangle abcd with side ab of length h inside along the axis and side cd outside. Label the enclosed turns nh and write Bh = μ0(nh)I beside it. Add a few curved lines at the ends to show the field spreading out.

At wire b show the field Ba of wire a as a cross (into the page) and the force Fba on b pointing towards a; at wire a show Bb as a dot and Fab pointing towards b. Write Fba/L = μ0IaIb/2πd and state that the wires attract. Optionally add a second pair with opposite currents and forces pointing away.

Mark the forces IbB on the two sides of length b, one out of and one into the page, and show the zero-force sides parallel to B. Draw a top view with the normal to the loop making angle θ with B and the perpendicular distance a sin θ between the two forces; write τ = IAB sin θ and the moment m = IA along the normal.

Label the phosphor-bronze suspension strip at the top with a mirror or pointer and a scale, the spring at the bottom, and the terminals T1, T2. Draw the field lines from N to S as radial lines converging towards the core, and label them radial magnetic field.

ncert_questions.q: A straight wire of mass 200 g and length 1.5 m carries a current of 2 A. It is suspended in mid-air by a uniform horizontal magnetic field B. What is the magnitude of the magnetic field?
ncert_questions.a:
For the wire to float, the upward magnetic force must balance its weight: BIl = mg (with the wire perpendicular to B, sin θ = 1).

B = mg/(Il) = (0.2 × 9.8)/(2 × 1.5) = 1.96/3 = 0.65 T.

The field must be horizontal and perpendicular to the wire, with its direction fixed by Fleming's left-hand rule so that the force is upward.

ncert_questions.q: If the magnetic field is parallel to the positive y-axis and a charged particle is moving along the positive x-axis, which way would the Lorentz force be for (a) an electron and (b) a proton?
ncert_questions.a:
v × B is along x̂ × ŷ = ẑ, the positive z-axis.

(a) For an electron the charge is negative, so the force is along −z (negative z-axis).

(b) For a proton the force is along +z (positive z-axis).

The magnitude in both cases is evB.

ncert_questions.q: A circular coil of wire consisting of 100 turns, each of radius 8.0 cm, carries a current of 0.40 A. What is the magnitude of the magnetic field B at the centre of the coil?
ncert_questions.a:
B = μ0NI/(2R) = (4π × 10−7 × 100 × 0.40)/(2 × 0.08) = (4π × 10−7 × 40)/0.16 = 4π × 10−7 × 250 = 3.14 × 10−4 T.

The field is along the axis of the coil, its sense given by the right-hand thumb rule.

ncert_questions.q: A long straight wire carries a current of 35 A. What is the magnitude of the field B at a point 20 cm from the wire?
ncert_questions.a:
B = μ0I/(2πr) = 2 × 10−7 × 35/0.20 = 3.5 × 10−5 T.

The field is tangential to a circle of radius 20 cm around the wire.

ncert_questions.q: A long straight wire in the horizontal plane carries a current of 50 A in the north to south direction. Give the magnitude and direction of B at a point 2.5 m east of the wire.
ncert_questions.a:
B = μ0I/(2πr) = 2 × 10−7 × 50/2.5 = 4 × 10−6 T.

Direction: take east as x̂, north as ŷ and vertically up as ẑ. The current is along −ŷ (north to south) and the point is along +x̂. The field is along (current) × (position) = (−ŷ) × x̂ = +ẑ, so B is vertically upward. Check with the right-hand thumb rule: thumb pointing south, the fingers curl upward on the east side of the wire.

ncert_questions.q: A horizontal overhead power line carries a current of 90 A in the east to west direction. What is the magnitude and direction of the magnetic field due to the current 1.5 m below the line?
ncert_questions.a:
B = μ0I/(2πr) = 2 × 10−7 × 90/1.5 = 1.2 × 10−5 T.

Direction: the current is along −x̂ (east to west), the point is along −ẑ (below). B is along (−x̂) × (−ẑ) = x̂ × ẑ = −ŷ, that is, towards the south.

ncert_questions.q: What is the magnitude of magnetic force per unit length on a wire carrying a current of 8 A and making an angle of 30° with the direction of a uniform magnetic field of 0.15 T?
A 3.0 cm wire carrying a current of 10 A is placed inside a solenoid perpendicular to its axis. The magnetic field inside the solenoid is given to be 0.27 T. What is the magnetic force on the wire?
ncert_questions.a:
The wire is perpendicular to the axis, hence to the field, so sin θ = 1.

F = BIl = 0.27 × 10 × 0.03 = 8.1 × 10−2 N, directed perpendicular to both the wire and the axis of the solenoid.

ncert_questions.q: Two long and parallel straight wires A and B carrying currents of 8.0 A and 5.0 A in the same direction are separated by a distance of 4.0 cm. Estimate the force on a 10 cm section of wire A.
ncert_questions.a:
Force per unit length f = μ0IAIB/(2πd) = 2 × 10−7 × 8 × 5/0.04 = 2 × 10−7 × 1000 = 2 × 10−4 N m−1.

Force on 10 cm: F = 2 × 10−4 × 0.10 = 2 × 10−5 N.

The currents are in the same direction, so the force is attractive, directed from A towards B.

ncert_questions.q: A closely wound solenoid 80 cm long has 5 layers of windings of 400 turns each. The diameter of the solenoid is 1.8 cm. If the current carried is 8.0 A, estimate the magnitude of B inside the solenoid near its centre.
ncert_questions.a:
Total turns N = 5 × 400 = 2000; length L = 0.80 m; n = N/L = 2500 turns per metre. The diameter is not needed since the field inside a long solenoid does not depend on it.

B = μ0nI = 4π × 10−7 × 2500 × 8.0 = 4π × 10−7 × 2 × 104 = 8π × 10−3 = 2.5 × 10−2 T.

ncert_questions.q: A square coil of side 10 cm consists of 20 turns and carries a current of 12 A. The coil is suspended vertically and the normal to the plane of the coil makes an angle of 30° with the direction of a uniform horizontal magnetic field of magnitude 0.80 T. What is the magnitude of torque experienced by the coil?
ncert_questions.a:
A = (0.10)2 = 0.01 m2; θ is between the normal and the field, 30°.

τ = NIAB sin θ = 20 × 12 × 0.01 × 0.80 × sin 30° = 1.92 × 0.5 = 0.96 N m.

ncert_questions.q: Two moving coil meters M<sub>1</sub> and M<sub>2</sub> have the following particulars: R<sub>1</sub> = 10 Ω, N<sub>1</sub> = 30, A<sub>1</sub> = 3.6 × 10<sup>−3</sup> m<sup>2</sup>, B<sub>1</sub> = 0.25 T; R<sub>2</sub> = 14 Ω, N<sub>2</sub> = 42, A<sub>2</sub> = 1.8 × 10<sup>−3</sup> m<sup>2</sup>, B<sub>2</sub> = 0.50 T (the spring constants are identical for the two meters). Determine the ratio of (a) current sensitivity and (b) voltage sensitivity of M<sub>2</sub> and M<sub>1</sub>.
ncert_questions.a:
(a) Current sensitivity Is = NAB/k. With equal k, Is2/Is1 = (N2A2B2)/(N1A1B1) = (42 × 1.8 × 0.50)/(30 × 3.6 × 0.25) = 37.8/27 = 1.4.

(b) Voltage sensitivity Vs = NAB/(kR). Vs2/Vs1 = 1.4 × (R1/R2) = 1.4 × 10/14 = 1.0.

M2 has 1.4 times the current sensitivity but the same voltage sensitivity as M1.

ncert_questions.q: In a chamber, a uniform magnetic field of 6.5 G (1 G = 10<sup>−4</sup> T) is maintained. An electron is shot into the field with a speed of 4.8 × 10<sup>6</sup> m s<sup>−1</sup> normal to the field. Explain why the path of the electron is a circle. Determine the radius of the circular orbit. (e = 1.6 × 10<sup>−19</sup> C, m<sub>e</sub> = 9.1 × 10<sup>−31</sup> kg)
ncert_questions.a:
The magnetic force ev × B is perpendicular to the velocity at every instant and has constant magnitude evB (v is perpendicular to B). It changes only the direction of v, so it acts as a centripetal force and the electron moves in a circle at constant speed in the plane perpendicular to B.

evB = mv2/r gives r = mv/(eB) = (9.1 × 10−31 × 4.8 × 106)/(1.6 × 10−19 × 6.5 × 10−4) = 4.37 × 10−24/1.04 × 10−22 = 4.2 × 10−2 m = 4.2 cm.

ncert_questions.q: In Exercise 4.11 obtain the frequency of revolution of the electron in its circular orbit. Does the answer depend on the speed of the electron? Explain.
ncert_questions.a:
ν = v/(2πr) = eB/(2πm) = (1.6 × 10−19 × 6.5 × 10−4)/(2π × 9.1 × 10−31) = 1.04 × 10−22/5.72 × 10−30 ≈ 1.8 × 107 Hz = 18 MHz.

The frequency does not depend on the speed: a faster electron moves on a proportionately larger circle (r ∝ v), so the time for one revolution, T = 2πm/(eB), is the same. This holds as long as the speed is much less than c so that m is constant.

ncert_questions.q: (a) A circular coil of 30 turns and radius 8.0 cm carrying a current of 6.0 A is suspended vertically in a uniform horizontal magnetic field of magnitude 1.0 T. The field lines make an angle of 60° with the normal of the coil. Calculate the magnitude of the counter torque that must be applied to prevent the coil from turning. (b) Would your answer change if the circular coil in (a) were replaced by a planar coil of some irregular shape that encloses the same area? (All other particulars are also unaltered.)
ncert_questions.a:
(a) A = πR2 = π × (0.08)2 = 2.01 × 10−2 m2.

Magnetic torque τ = NIAB sin θ = 30 × 6.0 × 2.01 × 10−2 × 1.0 × sin 60° = 3.62 × 0.866 = 3.1 N m. The counter torque needed is 3.1 N m, equal and opposite.

(b) No. The torque on a planar current loop depends only on the magnetic moment NIA, not on the shape of the loop. With the same area, turns, current and orientation the torque is unchanged.

pyq.q: A proton and an alpha particle enter a uniform magnetic field perpendicularly with the same speed. The ratio of the radii of their circular paths, r<sub>p</sub> : r<sub>α</sub>, is
pyq.answer: b
pyq.solution: r = mv/(qB), so for the same v, r ∝ m/q. For the alpha particle m/q = 4m<sub>p</sub>/2e = 2m<sub>p</sub>/e, twice that of the proton. Hence r<sub>p</sub> : r<sub>α</sub> = 1 : 2.

pyq.q: A charged particle moves through a region of uniform magnetic field with its velocity perpendicular to the field. Which of its physical quantities remains unchanged?
pyq.answer: c
pyq.solution: The magnetic force is always perpendicular to the velocity, so it does no work and the speed and kinetic energy stay constant. Velocity and momentum change in direction.

pyq.q: Two long parallel wires carry currents in opposite directions. The wires
options: experience a torque but no force
pyq.answer: b
pyq.solution: Antiparallel currents repel; parallel currents attract. The force per unit length is μ<sub>0</sub>I<sub>1</sub>I<sub>2</sub>/(2πd) in either case.

pyq.q: The magnetic field at the centre of a circular coil of N turns, radius R, carrying current I is
pyq.answer: b
pyq.solution: Putting x = 0 in the axial-field formula gives μ<sub>0</sub>I/(2R) per turn, and N turns add. Option (a) is the field of a straight wire at distance R; option (c) is the field of a semicircle.

pyq.q: A galvanometer of resistance G gives full-scale deflection for a current I<sub>g</sub>. To convert it into an ammeter of range 0 to I, the shunt required is
pyq.answer: b
pyq.solution: The shunt S is in parallel and carries I − I<sub>g</sub> while the coil carries I<sub>g</sub>; equal potential differences give I<sub>g</sub>G = (I − I<sub>g</sub>)S, so S = I<sub>g</sub>G/(I − I<sub>g</sub>).

pyq.q: The SI unit of magnetic field, the tesla, is equivalent to
pyq.answer: b
pyq.solution: From F = BIl, B = F/(Il), so 1 T = 1 N A<sup>−1</sup> m<sup>−1</sup>. Equivalently 1 T = 1 N s C<sup>−1</sup> m<sup>−1</sup> from F = qvB.

pyq.q: A current-carrying loop is placed in a uniform magnetic field. Which statement is correct?
options: It experiences a net force but no torque
It experiences a torque but no net force
It experiences neither a force nor a torque
It experiences both a net force and a torque
pyq.answer: b
pyq.solution: In a uniform field the forces on the elements of a closed loop add to zero, but the pair of forces on opposite sides forms a couple with torque NIAB sin θ, which is zero only when the normal is along B.

pyq.q: An electron is moving along the positive x-axis in a magnetic field directed along the positive z-axis. The force on the electron is along the
pyq.answer: a
pyq.solution: v × B = x̂ × ẑ = −ŷ. The electron is negative, so the force is opposite to this, along the positive y-axis.

pyq.q: Assertion (A): A charged particle projected perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field moves in a circle with constant speed. Reason (R): The magnetic force on a moving charge is always perpendicular to its velocity and does no work.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
pyq.answer: a
pyq.solution: The force q(v × B) is perpendicular to v, so it changes only the direction of the velocity; a constant-magnitude perpendicular force gives uniform circular motion. R is exactly the reason.

pyq.q: Assertion (A): The magnetic field inside a long straight solenoid carrying current is uniform. Reason (R): The magnetic field outside a long solenoid is nearly zero.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
pyq.answer: b
pyq.solution: Both statements are true, but the uniformity inside follows from the superposition of the fields of the turns (Ampere's law gives B = μ<sub>0</sub>nI independent of position); the weak field outside is a separate fact, not the cause.

pyq.q: Assertion (A): The scale of a moving coil galvanometer is linear. Reason (R): The concave pole pieces and the soft-iron core produce a radial magnetic field, so the torque on the coil is NIAB for every position of the coil.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
pyq.answer: a
pyq.solution: With a radial field sin θ = 1 always, so NIAB = kφ and φ ∝ I. The linear scale is a direct consequence of the radial field.

pyq.q: Assertion (A): A charged particle moving parallel to a uniform magnetic field experiences no force. Reason (R): The magnetic force is F = qvB sin θ, and sin 0° = 0.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
pyq.answer: a
pyq.solution: For v along B the angle θ is zero (or 180°) and the cross product v × B vanishes, so there is no force and the particle moves in a straight line.

pyq.q: Define one ampere in terms of the force between two parallel current-carrying conductors. Write the expression for the force per unit length on which the definition is based.
pyq.answer:
The force per unit length between two long straight parallel wires carrying currents I1 and I2 at separation d is f = μ0I1I2/(2πd).

One ampere is that steady current which, when maintained in each of two very long straight parallel conductors of negligible cross-section placed 1 m apart in vacuum, produces on each of them a force of 2 × 10−7 newton per metre of length.

pyq.q: An electron and a proton, having the same kinetic energy, enter a uniform magnetic field perpendicularly. Which of them describes the circle of larger radius? Justify.
pyq.answer:
r = mv/(qB) = √(2mK)/(qB), since mv = √(2mK).

For equal K and equal magnitude of charge, r ∝ √m. The proton is about 1836 times heavier, so it moves in the larger circle, rp/re = √(mp/me) ≈ 43.

pyq.q: Why is the magnetic field in a moving coil galvanometer made radial? How is it achieved?
pyq.answer:
In a radial field the plane of the coil is always parallel to the field lines, so the deflecting torque is NIAB (sin θ = 1) at every deflection. Then NIAB = kφ gives φ ∝ I, and the scale is linear.

It is achieved by using cylindrical (concave) pole pieces and placing a soft-iron cylinder inside the coil; the core also strengthens the field.

pyq.q: A beam of electrons moving horizontally from west to east enters a region where the magnetic field is directed vertically downward. In which direction is the beam deflected?
pyq.answer:
Take east as x̂ and vertically up as ẑ; then north is ŷ. Velocity is along +x̂ and B along −ẑ.

v × B = x̂ × (−ẑ) = +ŷ, towards north. The electron is negative, so the force on it is opposite, towards the south. The beam is deflected southward.

pyq.q: A straight wire of length 0.5 m carrying a current of 4 A is placed in a uniform magnetic field of 0.2 T. Find the force on the wire when it makes an angle of (i) 90° and (ii) 30° with the field.
pyq.answer:
F = BIl sin θ.

(i) F = 0.2 × 4 × 0.5 × 1 = 0.4 N.

(ii) F = 0.2 × 4 × 0.5 × sin 30° = 0.4 × 0.5 = 0.2 N.

The force is perpendicular to both the wire and the field.

pyq.q: Using Ampere's circuital law, obtain the magnetic field due to a long straight wire of radius a carrying a steady current I at a point (i) outside and (ii) inside the wire, the current being uniformly distributed over its cross-section. Draw the graph of B against the distance r from the axis.
pyq.answer:
Choose a circular Amperian loop of radius r coaxial with the wire; by symmetry B is constant on it and tangential, so ∮ B·dl = B(2πr).

(i) Outside, r ≥ a: the loop encloses the whole current I. B(2πr) = μ0I, so B = μ0I/(2πr). B ∝ 1/r.

(ii) Inside, r < a: the current density is I/(πa2), so the enclosed current is Ienc = I(πr2)/(πa2) = Ir2/a2. B(2πr) = μ0Ir2/a2, so B = μ0Ir/(2πa2). B ∝ r.

Graph: B rises linearly from zero at the axis to μ0I/(2πa) at r = a, then falls as 1/r. The field is maximum at the surface.

pyq.q: A long straight wire carries a current of 20 A. A rectangular loop PQRS carrying 10 A is placed in the same plane with its longer sides PQ and RS (each 20 cm) parallel to the wire, PQ at 2 cm from the wire and RS at 10 cm, the current in PQ being in the same direction as in the wire. Find the net force on the loop and state whether it is attracted or repelled.
pyq.answer:
Forces on the sides perpendicular to the wire (QR and SP) are equal and opposite, so they cancel.

Force on PQ (parallel currents, attractive, towards the wire): F1 = μ0I1I2L/(2πr1) = 2 × 10−7 × 20 × 10 × 0.20/0.02 = 4 × 10−4 N.

Force on RS (antiparallel currents, repulsive, away from the wire): F2 = 2 × 10−7 × 20 × 10 × 0.20/0.10 = 8 × 10−5 N.

Net force = F1 − F2 = 4 × 10−4 − 0.8 × 10−4 = 3.2 × 10−4 N, towards the wire. The loop is attracted. The net torque is zero because all forces lie in the plane of the loop.

pyq.q: Using Ampere's circuital law, derive an expression for the magnetic field inside a long straight solenoid having n turns per unit length and carrying a current I. Sketch the field lines.
pyq.answer:
Take a rectangular Amperian loop abcd with side ab (length h) inside the solenoid parallel to the axis and side cd outside.

∮ B·dl = ∫ab + ∫bc + ∫cd + ∫da. Along ab, B is parallel to dl: contribution Bh. Along bc and da, B is perpendicular to dl inside and zero outside: contribution zero. Along cd, B = 0 outside: contribution zero. So ∮ B·dl = Bh.

The loop encloses nh turns, so Ienc = nhI. Ampere's law: Bh = μ0nhI, giving B = μ0nI, independent of the position inside, hence uniform.

Field lines: straight, parallel, equally spaced lines along the axis inside; they spread out at the ends and close outside, resembling those of a bar magnet.

pyq.q: A galvanometer of resistance 15 Ω gives full-scale deflection for a current of 4 mA. How will you convert it into (i) an ammeter of range 0 to 6 A and (ii) a voltmeter of range 0 to 18 V?
pyq.answer:
(i) Ammeter: connect a shunt S in parallel. S = IgG/(I − Ig) = (4 × 10−3 × 15)/(6 − 0.004) = 0.06/5.996 = 1.0 × 10−2 Ω (about 0.01 Ω).

(ii) Voltmeter: connect a resistance R in series. R = V/Ig − G = 18/(4 × 10−3) − 15 = 4500 − 15 = 4485 Ω.

The ammeter (very low resistance) goes in series with the circuit; the voltmeter (very high resistance) goes in parallel across the element.

pyq.q: Two identical circular coils P and Q, each of radius R and carrying current I, are placed concentrically with their planes perpendicular to each other. Find the magnitude and direction of the net magnetic field at the common centre.
pyq.answer:
Each coil produces at its centre a field B0 = μ0I/(2R) along its own axis.

The two axes are perpendicular (the planes are perpendicular), so the fields are perpendicular vectors of equal magnitude. Net field B = √(B02 + B02) = √2 B0 = μ0I/(√2 R).

Direction: at 45° to the axis of either coil, in the plane containing the two axes, that is, tan θ = BQ/BP = 1.

pyq.q: State the Biot–Savart law. Use it to derive an expression for the magnetic field at a point on the axis of a circular current loop of radius R carrying current I, at a distance x from its centre. Hence write the field at the centre of the loop.
pyq.answer:
Biot–Savart law: the field of a current element I dl at a point at position r from it is dB = (μ0/4π) I (dl × r)/r3; magnitude dB = (μ0/4π) I dl sin θ/r2, direction perpendicular to the plane of dl and r.

Derivation: take the loop in the y–z plane centred at O, and P on the x-axis at distance x. For any element dl, r = √(x2 + R2) and dl ⊥ r, so dB = (μ0/4π) I dl/(x2 + R2).

dB is perpendicular to r; resolve it into dB cos α along the axis and dB sin α perpendicular to the axis, where cos α = R/√(x2 + R2). For the diametrically opposite element the perpendicular component is reversed, so all perpendicular components cancel and only the axial components add.

B = ∮ dB cos α = (μ0/4π) · I R/(x2 + R2)3/2 ∮ dl = (μ0/4π) · I R (2πR)/(x2 + R2)3/2.

Hence B = μ0IR2/[2(x2 + R2)3/2], along the axis, in the sense given by the right-hand thumb rule.

At the centre (x = 0): B = μ0I/(2R); for N turns, μ0NI/(2R).

pyq.q: (a) Derive an expression for the force per unit length between two long straight parallel conductors carrying currents I<sub>1</sub> and I<sub>2</sub> separated by a distance d. Hence define one ampere. (b) Two long parallel wires carrying 10 A and 20 A in the same direction are 5 cm apart. Find the force per unit length on each wire and state its nature.
pyq.answer:
(a) Wire 1 produces at wire 2 a field B1 = μ0I1/(2πd), perpendicular to wire 2. A length L of wire 2 in this field experiences F21 = I2LB1 = μ0I1I2L/(2πd). By F = I(L × B) this force is directed towards wire 1 when the currents are parallel. Similarly wire 1 experiences an equal force towards wire 2. So the force per unit length is f = μ0I1I2/(2πd), attractive for parallel and repulsive for antiparallel currents.

Putting I1 = I2 = 1 A, d = 1 m gives f = 2 × 10−7 N m−1. One ampere is that steady current which, maintained in each of two very long straight parallel conductors of negligible cross-section 1 m apart in vacuum, produces on each a force of 2 × 10−7 N per metre of length.

(b) f = 2 × 10−7 × 10 × 20/0.05 = 2 × 10−7 × 4000 = 8 × 10−4 N m−1 on each wire. The currents are parallel, so the force is attractive.

pyq.q: (a) Describe the principle, construction and working of a moving coil galvanometer with a labelled diagram. (b) Define current sensitivity and voltage sensitivity. Explain why increasing the current sensitivity does not necessarily increase the voltage sensitivity.
pyq.answer:
Principle: a current-carrying coil placed in a magnetic field experiences a torque.

Construction: a coil of N turns of insulated wire on a light rectangular frame, suspended by a phosphor-bronze strip (or pivoted between springs) between the concave pole pieces of a permanent magnet. A soft-iron cylinder is fixed inside the coil. The concave poles and the core make the field radial and strong. A mirror or pointer attached to the suspension reads the deflection on a scale. (Labelled diagram: N, S pole pieces; soft-iron core; coil; phosphor-bronze strip; spring; pointer and scale; terminals.)

Working: with current I, the deflecting torque is NIAB (sin θ = 1 because the field is radial). The suspension supplies a restoring torque kφ. At equilibrium NIAB = kφ, so φ = (NAB/k) I: the deflection is proportional to the current and the scale is linear.

Current sensitivity Is = φ/I = NAB/k, deflection per unit current. Voltage sensitivity Vs = φ/V = NAB/(kR), deflection per unit voltage, where R is the coil resistance.

Increasing N raises Is, but a longer wire raises R in the same proportion. Doubling N with the same wire doubles both NAB/k and R, so Vs = Is/R is unchanged. Hence a higher current sensitivity does not by itself mean a higher voltage sensitivity.

pyq.q: (a) Derive an expression for the torque acting on a rectangular current loop placed in a uniform magnetic field with its normal making an angle θ with the field. Express it in vector form and identify the magnetic moment of the loop. (b) A circular coil of 50 turns and radius 5 cm carrying 2 A is placed with its plane parallel to a field of 0.5 T. Find the torque on it.
pyq.answer:
(a) Let the loop have sides a and b and carry current I. When the normal makes angle θ with B, the sides of length b (perpendicular to B) experience equal and opposite forces F = IbB, into and out of the plane. The sides of length a experience equal, opposite and collinear forces that cancel. The two forces IbB form a couple whose arm is the perpendicular distance between their lines of action, a sin θ.

τ = IbB × a sin θ = IAB sin θ, with A = ab. For N turns, τ = NIAB sin θ.

Vector form: τ = m × B, where m = NIA is the magnetic moment of the loop, directed along the normal by the right-hand rule. Torque is zero when m is along B and maximum NIAB when the plane of the loop is parallel to B. The net force on the loop is zero.

(b) Plane parallel to the field means θ = 90°. A = π(0.05)2 = 7.85 × 10−3 m2. τ = NIAB = 50 × 2 × 7.85 × 10−3 × 0.5 = 0.39 N m.

pyq.q:
A moving coil galvanometer consists of a coil of many turns suspended in a radial magnetic field produced by concave pole pieces and a soft-iron core. When a current passes through the coil, it experiences a torque NIAB, balanced at equilibrium by the restoring torque kφ of the phosphor-bronze suspension. The deflection per unit current is the current sensitivity and the deflection per unit voltage is the voltage sensitivity. A galvanometer is very sensitive and cannot be used as such to measure the current in a circuit; it is converted into an ammeter by a shunt or into a voltmeter by a series resistance.
(i) Why is a soft-iron cylinder placed inside the coil?
(ii) Why cannot a galvanometer as such be used to measure the current in a circuit?
(iii) A galvanometer of resistance 20 Ω shows full-scale deflection at 5 mA. Find the shunt needed to convert it into an ammeter of range 1 A.
(iv) The number of turns of a galvanometer coil is doubled using the same wire. How do its current sensitivity and voltage sensitivity change?
pyq.answer:
(i) The soft-iron core concentrates the field lines, increasing B, and together with the concave pole pieces makes the field radial, so the torque is NIAB at all positions and the scale is linear.

(ii) It is very sensitive, giving full-scale deflection for currents of a few microamperes, so a circuit current would damage it; also its resistance is not negligible, so inserting it changes the current it is meant to measure.

(iii) S = IgG/(I − Ig) = (5 × 10−3 × 20)/(1 − 0.005) = 0.1/0.995 ≈ 0.10 Ω, connected in parallel.

(iv) Current sensitivity NAB/k doubles. The resistance also doubles with the doubled length of wire, so the voltage sensitivity NAB/(kR) stays the same.

pyq.q:
A charged particle entering a uniform magnetic field perpendicularly experiences a force qvB that is always perpendicular to its velocity. This force cannot change the speed of the particle; it only bends the path into a circle of radius r = mv/(qB). The time for one revolution, T = 2πm/(qB), does not depend on the speed. If the velocity has a component along the field, that component is unaffected and the path becomes a helix.
(i) How much work is done by the magnetic force on the particle in one revolution?
(ii) A proton (m = 1.67 × 10−27 kg) moves at 2 × 106 m s−1 perpendicular to a field of 0.1 T. Find the radius of its path.
(iii) Find the time period of the proton in (ii).
(iv) If the proton's speed is doubled, what happens to the radius and to the time period?
pyq.answer:
(i) Zero. The force is perpendicular to the displacement at every instant, so W = ∫ F·ds = 0 and the kinetic energy is unchanged.

(ii) r = mv/(qB) = (1.67 × 10−27 × 2 × 106)/(1.6 × 10−19 × 0.1) = 3.34 × 10−21/1.6 × 10−20 = 0.21 m.

(iii) T = 2πm/(qB) = (2π × 1.67 × 10−27)/(1.6 × 10−20) = 1.05 × 10−26/1.6 × 10−20 = 6.6 × 10−7 s.

(iv) The radius doubles (r ∝ v) to 0.42 m; the time period is unchanged because T does not depend on v.

common_mistakes: Forgetting the negative charge of the electron when finding the direction of the force: students correctly compute v × B and then leave the force along it. For an electron the force is opposite to v × B. The examiner deducts the direction mark.

Using the wrong angle in torque questions. In τ = NIAB sin θ the angle is between the normal to the coil and the field; if the plane of the coil makes 30° with the field, θ is 60°. NCERT exercise 4.9 and 4.13 both test exactly this.

Comparing radii of different particles without stating the condition. Same speed gives r ∝ m/q, same momentum gives r ∝ 1/q, same kinetic energy gives r ∝ √m/q. Mixing these up gives the wrong ratio for the proton–alpha pair, which is 1 : 2 at the same speed but 1 : 1 at the same energy.

Writing the Biot–Savart law without the sin θ factor or without the vector cross product, and drawing no figure. The derivation for the circular loop loses marks if the cancellation of the perpendicular components is not stated.

In the solenoid derivation, forgetting to explain why three sides of the Amperian rectangle contribute zero, or quoting B = μ0nI without the enclosed current nhI. The marking scheme gives separate marks for each step.

Saying that the magnetic force changes the speed or the kinetic energy of a charge. It never does; it changes only the direction. Any answer that talks about the field accelerating a particle to a higher speed is wrong.
Connecting the shunt in series or the voltmeter resistance in parallel, or dropping the −G term in R = V/Ig − G. Also using the full current I instead of I − Ig in the shunt formula.
Stating that the field of a long solenoid depends on its radius or on the distance from the axis, or forgetting that at the end the field is half the value at the centre.

Quoting 2 × 10<sup>−7</sup> N in the definition of the ampere but leaving out the conditions (very long, straight, parallel, negligible cross-section, 1 m apart, in vacuum, per metre of length). A definition without the conditions is usually given half marks.
strategy:
This chapter is built on four derivations and one instrument, and the paper almost always draws from them. Spend the first sitting on the derivations, writing each out on paper without looking: the axial field of a circular loop from the Biot–Savart law, the solenoid from Ampere's law, the force between parallel currents leading to the definition of the ampere, and the torque on a rectangular loop leading to τ = m × B. Each takes about ten minutes once you know the figure, and the figure is where the marks are. Draw the figure first every time.

The second sitting belongs to the moving coil galvanometer. Learn the principle, the labelled diagram, the equilibrium condition NIAB = kφ, both sensitivities, why the field is radial, why phosphor bronze, and the two conversions with their formulas. Then solve NCERT exercise 4.10 and one ammeter and one voltmeter numerical.

The third sitting is numericals: all thirteen NCERT exercises, then the ratio-of-radii questions in the three cases (same speed, same momentum, same energy), the rectangular loop near a straight wire, and Ampere's law inside a thick wire with the graph. Keep μ0/4π = 10−7 and 2 × 10−7 for the straight wire at your fingertips.

Note what is no longer in the syllabus: the cyclotron, the velocity selector, the toroid and the magnetic moment of a revolving electron were dropped in the rationalised NCERT, so do not spend time on them beyond knowing that the cyclotron frequency is qB/(2πm). Helical motion is still in Section 4.3 and is asked.

In the exam, write the formula, substitute with units, and state the direction of every vector answer. For any 5-mark derivation, the labelled figure plus the final boxed result should be on the page even if you run out of time in the middle.
